Define a partial DAG object without evaluating it

lazy_dag.Rd

This function should be used as a wrapper around an expression that aims to generate a DAG object, but with some parameters left un-specified. Those parameters should be defined using the param() syntax, as shown below. The DAG is then not instantly evaluated. Instead, it will only be evaluated later using a set_lazy_dag call, which then sets the still un-specified parameters. This may be useful to create flexible functions that generate DAG objects during simulations, and is also used in calibrate_dag.

Usage

lazy_dag(expr)

Arguments

expr

An expression that would usually create a DAG object. This should include one empty_dag call and one or more added node or node_td functions. Importantly, at least one parameter of one node should be left unspecified, using the param() syntax. See ?node for more information on how to specify a regular DAG. See details on how to use the param() syntax.

Details

It is sometimes convenient to define a DAG object, but to leave some parameters of it flexible. For example, if we wanted to conduct a Monte-Carlo simulation study with different values of an interaction coefficient in a formula of a node, we need different DAG definitions for each scenario. Instead of copying and pasting nearly the same code multiple times, this function allows users to define a single partially specified DAG that leaves one or multiple parameters of a DAG definition unspecified.

This works the same way a usual DAG construction does. The only two differences are (1) that the whole expression (expr) that creates the DAG should be wrapped in a lazy_dag() function call and (2) that parameters that should remain flexible are wrapped in a param() function. For example, if we wish to leave the intercept in a formula flexible, we could use param(intercept). There is no limit on the amount of flexible parameters that can be specified. They also do not have to be in a formula, but can be passed to any argument of any node call. The only requirements are that the names used inside the param() call are unique, so that they can later be unambiguously identified.

Once a lazy_DAG is created, users may create real DAG objects from it using the set_lazy_dag function, which only requires the lazy_DAG and a vector of params as input. See ?set_lazy_dag for more information. Before running set_lazy_dag(), it is not possible to use these objects to simulate any data, because they are not fully specified or even executed yet. Note also that param() is just a piece of syntax. The param() function itself does not actually exist in the simDAG package.

Value

Returns a lazy_DAG object.

Author

Robin Denz

Examples

library(simDAG)

# define a lazy DAG with one unspecified parameter
ldag <- lazy_dag(
  empty_dag() +
    node("A", type="rnorm", mean=1, sd=param(SD))
)

# get a real DAG object with SD = 1 and another with SD = 2
dag1 <- set_lazy_dag(ldag, params=c(SD=1))
dag2 <- set_lazy_dag(ldag, params=c(SD=2))

# define some lazy DAG, leaving the intercept of "death" and one beta
# coefficient of "smoking" unspecified
ldag <- lazy_dag(
  empty_dag() +
    node("age", type="rnorm", mean=10, sd=2) +
    node("sex", parents="", type="rbernoulli", p=0.5) +
    node("smoking", type="binomial",
         formula= ~ -2 + age*param(Sbeta) + sex*0.2) +
    node("death", type="binomial",
         formula= ~ param(Dintercept) + age*1 + sex*2)
)

# get a real DAG object from this with set values
dag3 <- set_lazy_dag(ldag, params=c(Sbeta=2.1, Dintercept=-10))
